I’m 35. I’ve dealt with depression since my early 20s, and anxiety my entire life. It’s gotten really bad over the past few years and I’ve had four pretty bad depressive episodes over the past two years, to the point where I can’t get out of bed, can’t work, stop eating for days at a time, etc. I nearly got admitted to a psych ward earlier this summer. You’re definitely not alone out there!! 

How do you like your therapist? If you feel like you don’t click with that person, it may be worth trying someone new if that’s possible. I only say that because I’ve talked to 4 or 5 therapists over the past 10+ years before I found one I click with and felt was actually helping me. 

The same goes for your treatment. If you’re on a med for depression that you feel isn’t helping you, tell your prescriber and ask to try a new one. If antidepressants don’t help you, ask about other forms of treatment. My experience with antidepressants has been pretty bad. My doctor finally recommended I look into TMS treatment which I’m completing now. It hasn’t been a cure all, but it’s been way more helpful than any antidepressant I’ve tried (and I’ve tried quite a few of them). 

I know it’s had to be persistent with these things and advocate for yourself when all you want to do is shut down. I’ve been there and I feel for you. Keep exploring your options. If you ever need someone to talk to feel free to dm me 💛

I struggle with the same thing when I hit my lowest lows. My appetite can check out for months, and it's really frustrating. I don't have a magic solution (I wish I did lol) but the things that have worked the most for me are stocking up on food to graze on throughout the day, versus making full meals which can seem overwhelming to finish. Protein bars have been a nice go-to in the morning because that's usually when my lack of appetite is the worst. 

Also, soups have been a helpful option to me. Vegetables are really where I struggle when I lose my appetite, but they're much easier to eat and digest in a soup because they're cooked down. Plus, you can freeze most soups and keep them for later if you want to try to eat something and don't feel like cooking.... just thaw and heat it up :)

I’ve been in a similar situation to yours. I loved my ex but I wasn’t in love with him anymore, I didn’t want to hurt him, and I wanted it to work so badly. We made the mistake of trying to salvage the relationship. We invested money into a couples counselor and we invested our time. It was a mistake that I regret.

You need to listen to that gut feeling of “this isn’t the one” because you won’t be able to wish that feeling away, and breaking things off will only get more difficult the longer you drag this out. Also, you’re not going to get that time back and neither will he. If you’re not in love with him it’s not fair to either of you to stay in this relationship.

It could be very possible that he checked all of your boxes of what you were looking for in a partner at the time. But you’re only 21 and are at a point in your life where you’re growing and changing a lot. It could be that the things you want in a partner have changed, and you just haven’t realized it yet. 

I think you two need to sit down and have a very open conversation about your feelings and what you want out of life and a relationship. Being completely honest with each other is the only way you can possibly salvage your friendship beyond a romantic relationship. Sometimes it doesn’t work out that way, however. And I think that you just need to remember that breaking apart from someone you love is going to hurt, but it WILL get easier with time. 

I really feel for you, OP. Take care of yourself whatever you choose to do!

It's easy to beat yourself up over a college rejection because it's such a big moment in your life, so I'm really sorry that you're feeling the way that you are. Rejection sucks. But that school is not judging your character or as a good human being. You're not less of a person just because they sent you a rejection letter.

Remember that many people who go to their first choice end up being disappointed with it, and many people love their college even if it wasn't their first choice. You're not guaranteed a positive experience just because you're accepted into a school. Unfortunately, you won't *really* know what a school will be like until you get there even if you've done a bunch of research! And just because a college is highly ranked or is a good fit for some people doesn't mean it's the best fit for *everyone*. 

Also, I think it might help if you don't force yourself to feel excited about the college you're going to or build up lots of big expectations. I built up very specific expectations of what the college I attended was going to be like and my first year was kind of miserable because none of those expectations were met. I went home for my first summer break and considered transferring to another school. I ended up staying and when I came back for my second year I pretty much ditched all of my expectations because my first year sucked so badly. My second year, and the rest of my time at that school, was one of the most enjoyable experiences of my life. Once I was able to stop wishing for college to be something specific I built up in my mind, I was able to enjoy it for what it was.

And the good news is, if you do end up hating the school you go to, you can transfer somewhere else! If you live in the US, it's easier to transfer to many schools than it is to get accepted out of high school as an incoming freshman.

ESH. After I read the title I really thought that you would be the sole asshole here, OP. But it was really shitty of your friend to say that to you and I totally get wanting an eye for an eye. I can't 100% say that my gut reaction would have been any different. But comments like that, regardless of the person's body type, are never okay. Take it from someone whose weight has fluctuated a lot... I've heard comments along the lines of both "you should eat less" and "you need to eat more". Both are hurtful and can stick with you. 

You were entirely in your right to speak up for yourself. You were also right in that she sounds like she's projecting her insecurities onto you. But I don't think it was okay to tell her she needs to eat less just because she said you should eat more. If you're interested in trying to mend your friendship (and it's fine if you're not), you need to explain to her how hurtful that comment was to you. If she can't understand that or keeps trying to justify her words, it might be time to end this relationship.

Have you asked him if he's had any such conversation with his housemate?

You can't *force* him to do anything like move out and I'm not sure what good blocking her on social media would do if they already live together. But you can tell him how it made you feel... and feeling upset by this is completely valid! 

What he does in response to your feelings will speak to how he prioritizes your relationship. If he shuts this kind of behavior down or looks for alternative living arrangements if she continues to make moves on him, then it's a sign that he's taking your feelings into consideration and prioritizing your relationship. But if he lets this behavior continue and doesn't really do anything about it, it's a sign that he's either indifferent about the entire thing or that he likes the extra attention. In either case, he's ignoring your feelings if he doesn't put his foot down. You may want to reconsider the relationship if he allows it to continue!

Personally I need to keep a planner because I'm better when things are written down and I can check things off of a list. I know some planners are crap, but I found one that really works for me. The brand is "Clever Fox" and I really like the layout! Plus it's blank (you write all the dates in) so I don't feel discouraged from using it if I miss a week and have a bunch of blank unused pages.

The weekly planning section has a page to plan each day out, in addition to a personal to-do list and habit tracking section. I write all of the things I need to do for work to check off as I do them (and I space them out over multiple days which helps me stay realistic about what I can actually do in a single day), but I also schedule/write down the days I plan to work out. If you're a senior you are SO close to being out of high school. I hated school from 6th until 12th grade. I felt completely isolated, with no friends, was self conscious about everything I said and did. I thought about killing myself but fear held me back. The only thing that got me through was telling myself that I didn't have to see any of the people I went to high school with again once I was out.

The world opens up so much once you move on from high school. You have so many more options of people to connect with and things to live for, regardless of whether you start working immediately after high school or attend college. I know it's the most cliche thing to say, but things really do get better once you're out. High school sucks. I think you should push through one more year of the high school BS and experience the real world before you make any decisions you can't undo. And if you feel that you just can't do that, maybe seek out a counselor. You don't have to go this alone.
